value.overview: The Pheasant Cuckoo is a large, secretive Neotropical cuckoo named for its exceptionally long, graduated tail. It spends much of its time walking quietly through dense ground vegetation and leaf litter, so it is usually heard rather than seen. Its distinctive song consists of clear whistles followed by a trill. Unlike many familiar cuckoos, it is strongly associated with forest understory and thick secondary growth across Central and South America.
value.classification: The Pheasant Cuckoo belongs to the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, and the ground-cuckoo subfamily Neomorphinae. Its scientific name is Dromococcyx phasianellus.
value.identification: This cuckoo has dark brown to sooty upperparts, pale buff underparts, and a long, broad, pheasant-like tail with graduated feathers. The head is relatively small and bears a short rusty-tipped crest that may be raised when the bird is alert. The breast is finely streaked or spotted with dark markings. The iris and bare eye-ring are yellowish to greenish yellow. It is difficult to observe because it moves stealthily through dense vegetation and often remains concealed.
value.rangeHabitat: The Pheasant Cuckoo occurs from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America. In Costa Rica it is regarded as a resident, with a broad but very local and apparently rare distribution, especially in lowlands along the Pacific slope; it has been recorded locally up to about 800 meters. It uses dense forest understory, riverine forest, forest edges, secondary growth, scrubby woodland, and other areas with thick ground cover.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident rather than migratory. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round, although its unobtrusive habits and seasonal singing may make it seem absent outside the main vocal period.
value.breeding: The Pheasant Cuckoo is a brood parasite and lays its egg in the nest of another bird, leaving the host to provide parental care. Reported or suspected hosts include several small flycatchers, such as Myiozetetes species, Rhynchocyclus flycatchers, and the Pied Water-Tyrant, as well as the Barred Antshrike. Details of its breeding cycle remain poorly known. In Costa Rica, parasitism has been associated with nests of broad-billed or related flycatchers.
value.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on insects and other small animals found on or near the ground. Recorded prey includes grasshoppers, cicadas, beetles, and other arthropods; small lizards and nestlings may also be taken occasionally. While foraging, it walks through leaf litter and low vegetation, sometimes vibrating its plumage, clapping its bill, or bobbing its body and tail before making a short rush to seize prey.
value.behavior: The species is usually solitary or found in pairs and is notably elusive. It forages terrestrially in dense cover but often sings from a low or middle-height perch in the understory or from the ground. Its loud, distinctive song is more frequently detected than the bird itself, especially during the breeding season. The rusty crest may be raised during excitement, and the long tail is often conspicuous when the bird crosses an opening.

conservation.populationTrend: A precise global population estimate and well-supported population trend are not available. The species remains widespread, although it is locally uncommon and difficult to detect.
